elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: New Section 11.4: "Corio, as Commerce One's customer under this Agreement, may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One". The element is disjunctive (Agreement or Order Form) and this contract has no Order Form structure, so the Agreement-level right suffices.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: 11.4 requires "thirty (30) days' prior written notice to Commerce One" — exactly the 30-day ceiling, in writing, running from Customer's notice.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: 11.4: "Commerce One shall refund pro rata any prepaid fees for the period after the effective date of termination." The words "pro rata" are express, not merely inferred from a post-termination period.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: 11.4: "Commerce One shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the initial five (5) year term or any renewal term." Retained 11.2 gives Commerce One only for-cause/insolvency exits, and the 30-day notice in 11.1 is a natural-term non-renewal tied to expiration of the then-current term (RENEWAL, not mid-term T4C), so no retained sentence contradicts 11.4.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: 11.4 sets thirty (30) days' notice, which is outside the literal 60–90 day fallback band (it is the preferred, more Customer-favourable figure).

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: no early-termination fee, penalty, or accelerated-payment mechanic is imposed anywhere in Section 11 or in the inserted 11.4, so the three-month ceiling is satisfied a fortiori.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply in a stricter form: 11.4 gives Commerce One no convenience right at all during the initial or any renewal term, and 11.1's non-renewal notice operates only at expiration of the then-current term.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: Commerce One has no convenience termination right to exercise under 11.4, so no notice floor is triggered; the 30-day notice in 11.1 is a natural-term non-renewal mechanic assessed under RENEWAL.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: the inserted Section 11.4 carries all four preferred elements (Customer convenience right, 30 days' written notice, express pro rata refund of prepaid fees, and an express bar on Vendor convenience termination during the initial and renewal terms).

The 'Customer convenience termination present' regex returning false reflects the baseline document (and the fact that the Customer is named 'Corio' rather than a playbook alias); inspected in substance, the rendered 11.4 plainly grants Corio a convenience exit, so the mechanical miss does not defeat coverage.

Minimality holds: existing 11.1–11.3 are untouched, no favourable language is deleted, the model-language surplus 'in whole or in part' was correctly omitted because there is no Order Form or partial-termination structure, and no survival tail, expense, or procedural extras were added. The short appositive 'as Commerce One's customer under this Agreement' is a lowercase descriptor that does not invoke the defined term CUSTOMER(S) in Section 1.6 and imposes no operative requirement; it is at most cosmetic.

Intent preserved: Section 11.3's survival list (4.2, 5.3, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14) and the Corio Customer/support carve-outs continue to operate on any termination including one under 11.4; the new section number 11.4 creates no dangling cross-reference and no retained sentence contradicts the new right.

Fallback is not independently complete because notice is 30 days rather than 60–90, but that is irrelevant to position-completeness since the preferred checklist is fully met; the comment's offer to move to 60–90 days is a negotiation concession, not an operative gap.
Finding status 'deviation' is correct: the original Section 11 gave Corio no convenience exit across a five-year committed term, failing even the fallback.
